questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $T : \mathbb{R}^7 \to \mathbb{R}^4$ be a surjective linear transformation. What is the dimension of $\ker(T)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $T$ is surjective onto $\mathbb{R}^4$, $\operatorname{rank}(T) = \dim(\operatorname{im}(T)) = 4$. By the Rank-Nullity Theorem, $\dim(\ker(T)) = \dim(\mathbb{R}^7) - \operatorname{rank}(T) = 7 - 4 = 3$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be a $6$-dimensional real vector space and let $W$ be a $2$-dimensional subspace of $V$. What is the dimension of the annihilator $W^0 = \{f \in V^* : f(w) = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}$?
questions.explanationEn: For any subspace $W$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$, $\dim(W) + \dim(W^0) = \dim(V)$. Thus $\dim(W^0) = 6 - 2 = 4$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $W = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 0, 0), (0, 1, 1, 0), (1, 2, 1, 0)\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^4$ with the standard inner product. What is $\dim(W^\perp)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $(1, 2, 1, 0) = (1, 1, 0, 0) + (0, 1, 1, 0)$ while the first two vectors are linearly independent, $\dim(W) = 2$. Hence $\dim(W^\perp) = \dim(\mathbb{R}^4) - \dim(W) = 4 - 2 = 2$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $\mathcal{B} = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}$ be an ordered basis of $\mathbb{R}^2$. What is the coordinate vector $[v]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of $v = (5, 1)$?
questions.explanationEn: Solve $c_1(1, 1) + c_2(1, -1) = (5, 1)$, giving $c_1 + c_2 = 5$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 1$. Adding yields $2c_1 = 6 \implies c_1 = 3$, and subtracting yields $2c_2 = 4 \implies c_2 = 2$. Thus $[v]_{\mathcal{B}} = (3, 2)^T$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^8$ with $\dim(U) = 5$, $\dim(W) = 4$, and $\dim(U + W) = 7$. Then $\dim(U \cap W)$ is equal to
questions.explanationEn: By Grassmann's dimension formula, $\dim(U + W) = \dim(U) + \dim(W) - \dim(U \cap W)$, so $\dim(U \cap W) = 5 + 4 - 7 = 2$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be the real vector space of all real sequences $(a_n)_{n=0}^{\infty}$ satisfying $a_{n+3} = 2a_{n+2} - a_{n+1} + 5a_n$ for all $n \ge 0$. What is $\dim_{\mathbb{R}}(V)$?
questions.explanationEn: Every sequence in $V$ is uniquely determined by its initial triple $(a_0, a_1, a_2) \in \mathbb{R}^3$, and any triple $(a_0, a_1, a_2) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ generates a unique sequence in $V$ via the recurrence. Thus the map $(a_n) \mapsto (a_0, a_1, a_2)$ is a linear isomorphism $V \cong \mathbb{R}^3$, so $\dim_{\mathbb{R}}(V) = 3$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $T : P_3(\mathbb{R}) \to P_3(\mathbb{R})$ be the invertible linear operator $T(p)(x) = p(x) + p'(x)$. What is $T^{-1}(x^3)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $T = I + D$ and $D^4 = 0$ on $P_3(\mathbb{R})$, we have $T^{-1} = I - D + D^2 - D^3$. Applying this to $x^3$ yields $x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6$. Directly checking: $(x^3 - 3x^2 + 6x - 6) + (3x^2 - 6x + 6) = x^3$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Applying the Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization process (without normalization) to the ordered list $v_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, $v_2 = (1, 0, 1)$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the standard inner product yields the second orthogonal vector $u_2$ equal to
questions.explanationEn: With $u_1 = v_1 = (1, 1, 0)$, we have $\langle v_2, u_1 \rangle = 1$ and $\langle u_1, u_1 \rangle = 2$. Hence $u_2 = v_2 - \frac{\langle v_2, u_1 \rangle}{\langle u_1, u_1 \rangle} u_1 = (1, 0, 1) - \frac{1}{2}(1, 1, 0) = \left(\frac{1}{2}, -\frac{1}{2}, 1\right)$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Does there exist a linear transformation $T : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ such that $T(1, 1, 0) = (2, 1)$, $T(0, 1, 1) = (1, -1)$, and $T(1, 2, 1) = (3, c)$? If so, what must $c$ be, and is $T$ unique?
optionsEn: No such linear transformation exists for any $c \in \mathbb{R}$.
$c = 0$, and there are infinitely many such linear transformations $T$.
questions.explanationEn: Observe that $(1, 2, 1) = (1, 1, 0) + (0, 1, 1)$. By linearity, $T(1, 2, 1) = T(1, 1, 0) + T(0, 1, 1) = (2, 1) + (1, -1) = (3, 0)$, which forces $c = 0$. Since $\{(1, 1, 0), (0, 1, 1)\}$ spans only a $2$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3$, we can extend it to a basis by adding $(0, 0, 1)$ and assign $T(0, 0, 1)$ arbitrarily in $\mathbb{R}^2$, yielding infinitely many such linear maps.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $T : \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be defined by $T(x, y) = (2x + 3y, x + 4y)$. What is the matrix representation $[T]_{\mathcal{B}}$ of $T$ with respect to the ordered basis $\mathcal{B} = \{(1, 1), (1, -1)\}$?
questions.explanationEn: Evaluate $T$ on the basis vectors: $T(1, 1) = (5, 5) = 5(1, 1) + 0(1, -1)$ and $T(1, -1) = (-1, -3) = -2(1, 1) + 1(1, -1)$. Placing these coordinate vectors as columns gives $[T]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{pmatrix} 5 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $T : \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be a linear transformation. Which of the following statements is/are ALWAYS TRUE?
questions.explanationEn: Since $\operatorname{rank}(T) \le \dim(\mathbb{R}^3) = 3$, Rank-Nullity gives $\dim(\ker(T)) = 4 - \operatorname{rank}(T) \ge 1$, so $T$ is never injective; thus (A) and (B) are TRUE. $T$ need not be surjective (e.g., $T = 0$), so (C) is FALSE. If $\dim(\ker(T)) = 1$, then $\operatorname{rank}(T) = 4 - 1 = 3 = \dim(\mathbb{R}^3)$, so $T$ is surjective; thus (D) is TRUE.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $V = \mathbb{R}^3$ and consider the linear functionals $f_1(x, y, z) = x + y$, $f_2(x, y, z) = y + z$, and $f_3(x, y, z) = x - z$ in $V^*$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
optionsEn: $\{f_1, f_2, f_3\}$ is a basis of $V^*$.
$\{f_1, f_2, f_3\}$ is linearly dependent in $V^*$.
questions.explanationEn: Notice that $f_1 - f_2 = (x + y) - (y + z) = x - z = f_3$, so $\{f_1, f_2, f_3\}$ is linearly dependent (making (B) TRUE and (A) FALSE). Because $f_3 = f_1 - f_2$, any $v \in \ker(f_1) \cap \ker(f_2)$ satisfies $f_3(v) = 0$, so (D) is TRUE. Since $f_1$ and $f_2$ are linearly independent, $\dim(\ker(f_1) \cap \ker(f_2) \cap \ker(f_3)) = 3 - 2 = 1$, making (C) TRUE.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $U$ and $W$ be subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^7$ such that $\dim(U) = 4$ and $\dim(W) = 5$. Which of the following values is/are possible for $\dim(U \cap W)$?
questions.explanationEn: Since $U + W \subseteq \mathbb{R}^7$, $\dim(U + W) \le 7$, so $\dim(U \cap W) = \dim(U) + \dim(W) - \dim(U + W) \ge 4 + 5 - 7 = 2$. Also, $U \cap W \subseteq U$ implies $\dim(U \cap W) \le \dim(U) = 4$. Every integer in $\{2, 3, 4\}$ is attainable by choosing bases of $U$ and $W$ sharing $2$, $3$, or $4$ vectors. Thus (B), (C), and (D) are correct.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $u = (1, 2, -1)^T$ and $v = (2, 1, 4)^T$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and define $T : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ by $T(x) = (v^T x) u$. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanationEn: Since $u, v \neq 0$, $\operatorname{im}(T) = \operatorname{span}\{u\}$ has dimension $1$, so $\operatorname{rank}(T) = 1$ ((A) TRUE). Next, $v^T u = 2(1) + 1(2) + 4(-1) = 0$, so $\operatorname{tr}(T) = v^T u = 0$ ((D) FALSE). Consequently, $T(u) = (v^T u)u = 0$, which means $u \in \ker(T)$, so $\operatorname{im}(T) \subseteq \ker(T)$ and $T^2 = 0$ ((B) and (C) TRUE).

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: What is the dimension of the real vector space $\operatorname{Hom}(P_2(\mathbb{R}), M_2(\mathbb{R}))$ of all linear transformations from $P_2(\mathbb{R})$ to $M_2(\mathbb{R})$? _________
questions.explanationEn: Since $\dim P_2(\mathbb{R}) = 3$ and $\dim M_2(\mathbb{R}) = 4$, we have $\dim \operatorname{Hom}(P_2(\mathbb{R}), M_2(\mathbb{R})) = 3 \times 4 = 12$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $W \subseteq M_4(\mathbb{R})$ be the subspace of all $4 \times 4$ Toeplitz matrices, i.e., matrices $(a_{ij})$ such that $a_{ij} = a_{i+1, j+1}$ for all $1 \le i, j \le 3$. Then $\dim(W)$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanationEn: In a $4 \times 4$ Toeplitz matrix, entries are constant along every diagonal $i - j = k$. Since $k = i - j$ takes the $7$ distinct integer values $-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3$, there are $7$ independent parameters, so $\dim(W) = 7$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: In $\mathbb{C}^2$ with the standard Hermitian inner product $\langle u, v \rangle = u_1\overline{v_1} + u_2\overline{v_2}$, if $u = (1, i)$ and $v = (2i, k)$ (with $k \in \mathbb{R}$) are orthogonal, then $k$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanationEn: We compute $\langle u, v \rangle = 1 \cdot \overline{(2i)} + i \cdot \overline{k} = -2i + ik = i(k - 2)$. Setting $\langle u, v \rangle = 0$ gives $k = 2$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $T : \mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}^3$ be the linear transformation represented by the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 7 \\ 3 & 6 & 4 & 10 \end{pmatrix}$. Then the nullity of $T$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanationEn: Notice that Row 3 equals Row 1 plus Row 2, while Row 1 and Row 2 are linearly independent (since the $2 \times 2$ minor from columns $1$ and $3$ is $1(3) - 1(2) = 1 \neq 0$). Thus $\operatorname{rank}(T) = 2$, and by Rank-Nullity, $\operatorname{nullity}(T) = 4 - 2 = 2$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $W$ be the subspace of all odd polynomials in $P_7(\mathbb{R})$. Then the dimension of the quotient vector space $P_7(\mathbb{R}) / W$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanationEn: We have $\dim P_7(\mathbb{R}) = 8$, and $W = \operatorname{span}\{x, x^3, x^5, x^7\}$ has dimension $4$. Thus $\dim(P_7(\mathbb{R})/W) = 8 - 4 = 4$.

questions.pyqTag: IIT JAM MA Topic • Vector Spaces & Linear Transformations (Set 02)
questions.questionTextEn: Let $V$ be the real vector space of all continuously differentiable ($C^1$) functions $f : [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$ whose restriction to each of the three subintervals $\left[0, \frac{1}{3}\right]$, $\left[\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right]$, and $\left[\frac{2}{3}, 1\right]$ is a polynomial of degree at most $2$. Then $\dim(V)$ is equal to _________.
questions.explanationEn: On each of the $3$ subintervals, a polynomial of degree at most $2$ has $3$ coefficients, giving $3 \times 3 = 9$ parameters in total. Continuity of $f$ and $f'$ at the two interior nodes $x = \frac{1}{3}$ and $x = \frac{2}{3}$ imposes $2 \times 2 = 4$ linearly independent homogeneous linear constraints (alternatively, a basis is $\{1, x, x^2, (x - 1/3)_+^2, (x - 2/3)_+^2\}$). Hence $\dim(V) = 9 - 4 = 5$.
